passages.happening:
The heads of the clan of Gilead, of the tribe of Manasseh, come to Moses and the leaders (verse 1). They recall that God commanded Moses to give the land of their relative Zelophehad to his daughters (verse 2).

They see a difficulty. “But if they marry any of the men from the other tribes of Israel, their inheritance will be withdrawn from the portion of our fathers and added to the tribe into which they marry” (verse 3). Even the Jubilee would not bring it back (verse 4).
passages.hearers:
The book ends where its last section began, with the daughters of Zelophehad. In chapter 27 the five sisters asked for their father's land, and God said they were right. Now their wider family raises a question that follows from that ruling.

The question is a real one. Land in Israel was a family's living, its place in the community and its name. A tribe's territory meant the same on a larger scale. And marriage ordinarily took a woman into her husband's family, with any property she brought. If a woman who had inherited land married a man of another tribe, her father's fields would pass, through her children, to her husband's tribe. Over the generations a tribe's land could be worn away piece by piece.

The clan leaders mention the Jubilee, the fiftieth year of Leviticus 25, when land that had been sold went back to its first family. They see that it would not help them. The Jubilee reversed sales. Land that passed by marriage and inheritance would stay where it had gone.

Notice how the matter is handled. The elders do not question the earlier ruling. They do not say that the daughters should not have been given the land. They begin by repeating what God commanded, and they ask how it fits with another thing God commanded, that each tribe should keep its inheritance. They bring the problem to Moses, as the sisters did, and wait for an answer.

This is the last of several stories in Numbers in which a case that the law has not covered is brought forward and a new ruling is given. The book shows God's law as something that answers real questions as they arise among his people.
passages.later:
The Jubilee law gives the reason land could never finally be lost to a family: “The land must not be sold permanently, because it is Mine, and you are but foreigners and residents with Me” (Leviticus 25:23).

The same care for a family's land appears in the story of Naboth, who refused to sell his vineyard even to a king: “The LORD forbid that I should give you the inheritance of my fathers” (1 Kings 21:3).
passages.asks: The elders of Gilead brought a hard question openly and waited for God's answer. Ask what follows from a good decision you have made that you have not yet thought through. And ask whether you raise such questions in a way that honors what has already been decided.

passages.t: Each tribe keeps its inheritance, and the sisters obey
passages.happening:
Moses answers ‘at the word of the LORD’: “The tribe of the sons of Joseph speaks correctly” (verse 5).

“This is what the LORD has commanded concerning the daughters of Zelophehad: They may marry anyone they please, provided they marry within a clan of the tribe of their father” (verse 6). The rule is made general. A daughter who inherits land is to marry within her father's tribe, ‘for each tribe of Israel must retain its inheritance’ (verses 8-9).

“So the daughters of Zelophehad did as the LORD had commanded Moses. Mahlah, Tirzah, Hoglah, Milcah, and Noah, the daughters of Zelophehad, were married to cousins on their father’s side” (verses 10-11). Their land stayed in their father's tribe (verse 12).

The book closes: “These are the commandments and ordinances that the LORD gave the Israelites through Moses on the plains of Moab by the Jordan across from Jericho” (verse 13).
passages.hearers:
God's answer uses the words he used of the sisters in chapter 27. They ‘speak correctly’, he said then. Now the clan ‘speaks correctly’. Both sides are told that they are right, and the two rulings are made to fit together. The daughters keep their land, and the tribe keeps its territory.

The ruling limits the sisters' choice, and that should be said. They may marry ‘anyone they please’, and the text says so in those words. No husband is chosen for them. But the choice must fall within their father's tribe. The law works inside the order of its world, in which land belonged to tribes and marriage carried property with it. It is a rule about heiresses and tribal land in ancient Israel. It is not a rule about whom anyone may marry today.

Marriage between cousins was common and accepted in that world, and it was a usual way of keeping property in a family.

The key word of the chapter is ‘inheritance’. It comes seventeen times in thirteen verses, more thickly than anywhere else in the book. Twice the text says that each tribe is to ‘retain’ its inheritance. The Hebrew verb means to cling or hold fast. It is the verb used in Genesis for a man holding fast to his wife, and in Deuteronomy for Israel holding fast to the LORD.

Then come the last events the book records. Five women do what God commanded, and they are named once more, each one. Numbers has told of forty years of complaint and revolt. The first generation was counted at Sinai and died in the desert because it would not trust God for the land. The book's final scene belongs to five daughters of that generation, who asked for a share in the land before a field of it had been won, and who then kept God's word about it. Their trust is the answer to the unbelief of Kadesh.

The middle of the book was full of deaths in the wilderness. Its last chapter speaks only of inheritance. It ends, as its second half began, on the plains of Moab across from Jericho, with the river still to cross. The story goes on in Deuteronomy, where Moses speaks to this generation on these same plains, and in Joshua, where the people cross.
passages.later:
The book of Joshua records the end of the sisters' story. They came to Eleazar and Joshua and reminded them of God's command. “So Joshua gave them an inheritance among their father’s brothers, in keeping with the command of the LORD” (Joshua 17:4).

The New Testament speaks of an inheritance that cannot be lost by sale, by marriage or by death. Peter calls it ‘an inheritance that is imperishable, undefiled, and unfading, reserved in heaven for you’ (1 Peter 1:4). Paul says that believers are ‘heirs of God and co-heirs with Christ’ (Romans 8:17), and that people of every nation share it: “the Gentiles are fellow heirs, fellow members of the body, and fellow partakers of the promise in Christ Jesus” (Ephesians 3:6).
passages.hard:
Is it fair that the sisters, having won their inheritance, were then told whom they could marry?

A reader may feel that something given in chapter 27 is partly taken back here. The feeling is reasonable. The sisters gain land that custom would have denied them, and then their freedom to marry is narrowed for the sake of that land.

Two things can be said. The ruling protects the sisters' gain as well as the tribe's. Their father's name and fields stay together, which is what they asked for. And the limit left them a real choice among many families.

But the law does not treat women and men alike, and it should not be read as if it did. It belongs to a world in which land was held by tribes and passed through men. The note on 27:1-11 sets out how readers weigh that. Nothing in this chapter gives any family today the right to choose a woman's husband, to forbid her marriage for the sake of property, or to pressure her into one.

If you are being hurt, at home, at work or in a church, tell someone you trust and get help. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: The book of the wilderness ends with five women who trusted God for an inheritance and then did as he said. Ask what you are trusting God for that you cannot yet see. And ask, at the end of this book, which generation you belong to: the one that looked at the land and turned back, or the one that asked for its share and crossed over.
